title: The Multiple You Get Is Set Years Before You Ever List the Business
linkedin:
Most owners assume valuation prep starts the day they decide to sell.

By then, a lot of the number is already locked in.

A buyer, or the valuer working on their behalf, isn't pricing last year's profit. They're pricing the pattern behind it. How consistent earnings have been across several years. How much revenue still runs through the owner personally. How concentrated the customer base has become. How well the business would survive a change of hands.

None of that shows up convincingly in a single year of tidy financial statements, no matter how well they're presented.

A pre sale clean up genuinely helps. It tidies presentation and removes obvious distractions for due diligence. What it can't do is manufacture three years of consistent trading history, spread a customer base that's drifted toward one or two large accounts, or prove the business runs without the owner in a matter of months.

Those patterns take years to build. Buyers are specifically looking for the years, not the months.

October carries a different kind of energy to EOFY, more forward looking, a chance to look three to five years out rather than just close the books on the year behind. It's a genuinely good prompt to ask which of those years is starting now, long before a buyer is ever in the room.

Full piece on the ProfitPulse blog.

Question for any business owner who's thought "I'll sort the numbers out properly when I actually decide to sell."

Worth knowing: the six months before a sale can tidy up presentation, but it can't manufacture three years of consistent earnings, spread out a customer base that leans on one or two big accounts, or prove the business runs fine without you. Those things take actual years to build, not months.

Doesn't matter if selling is nowhere near the radar right now. The habits that eventually lift the number are pretty much just what good ongoing management looks like anyway.

Anyone here started "exit proofing" years before they had any real plan to sell?

A quick thought for business owners on the East Coast this October, whether or not selling is anywhere on your radar.

We're often asked how to lift a business's value in the months before a sale. The honest answer is that a lot of what a buyer prices, consistent earnings across several years, a customer base that isn't leaning on one or two big accounts, and a business that doesn't depend heavily on the owner personally, takes years to build, not months. A tidy up right before a sale helps with presentation, but it can't manufacture that history after the fact.

October tends to bring a different kind of energy than the end of financial year rush, more forward looking, a good moment to think three to five years ahead rather than just closing the books on the year just gone.

If that's a conversation worth having for your business, whether you're planning to sell next year or simply want to understand where things stand today, it's worth starting now rather than waiting for a reason to rush it.

Read the full piece on the blog for more on what actually moves the number.
